2. BRIEF FACTS (a) Preliminary information regarding the accident in question was received at PS Lajpat Nagar vide GD No. 3A dated 03.06.2020 from AIIMS Trauma Center concerning the MLC of the injured person.

Upon receipt of the said information, the Investigating Officer (IO) proceeded to AIIMS Trauma Center and collected the MLC of the injured Shankar, which contained the description of road traffic accident noted by doctor.
The IO also obtained the MLC of the respondent no. 1/driver of the offending vehicle; however, the doctor opined that he was not fit for giving a statement at that time.
Thereafter, the IO visited the residence of the injured, where the injured narrated the facts of the accident and submitted a written complaint.
In his complaint, the injured stated that on 02.06.2020 at about 09:30 PM, he had MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors.

(a) A joint Written Statement/Reply was filed on behalf of Respondent No. 1 (the driver) and Respondent No. 2 (the owner), wherein they contended that they have been falsely implicated in the present case.
It was asserted that no accident occurred due to any rash or negligent driving on the part of Respondent No. 1.

On the contrary,

Consequently, when Respondent No. 1 applied sudden brakes, he lost balance and the motorcycle collided with the injured.

(b) A Reply/Written Statement was also filed on behalf of the Insurance Company,
wherein a statutory defence was raised to the effect that the driver of the offending vehicle was not holding a valid and effective driving licence at the time of the alleged accident.
It was further pointed out that relevant provisions regarding driving without a valid licence were added in the charge sheet.

It was contended that it is the bounden duty of the owner to ensure, before handing over the offending vehicle, that the driver possesses a valid driving licence, and that Respondent MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Accordingly, it was prayed that the Insurance Company be exonerated from liability.

It was further stated that the claimant himself contributed to the accident, as he attempted to cross a busy Ring Road, where high- speed traffic normally passes, despite the presence of a nearby foot overbridge, thereby putting his life in peril.
However, the validity and genuineness of the insurance policy were conceded.

Issue No.1 i).

The driver of the motorcycle,

During cross- examination, the driver admitted that he did not hold a valid driving license on the date of the accident, and he procured the license only after the incident.
He stated that the speed of his vehicle was around 40-50 kmph at the time and denied that he was driving at 80-100 kmph or in a zig-zag manner.

(e) The mechanical inspection report on record reflects fresh damages and scratches primarily on the left side of the motorcycle, indicating and confirming the collision.
It significant to note that the driver did not possess a valid license at the time, which strongly indicates a lack of sufficient experience to operate the vehicle safely.
It is highly unlikely that an experienced rider would drive for years without a license and then apply for driving license for the first time only after an accident.

In this case, since the driver obtained his license for the first time post-accident, it is reasonable to infer that he lacked the skill and adequate experience to safely navigate the vehicle on the inner Ring Road, a major circular arterial road that connects various parts of Delhi and carries heavy and diverse traffic at all hours.
It is also right to mention here that the make of offending motorcycle was Bajaj KTM 125 Duke, a vehicle widely recognized for its high-speed performance and agility.

(f) Further, even if the injured jumped suddenly in front of the motorcycle, a competent and experienced driver, especially one driving in a congested urban area, is expected to anticipate hazards, maintain a safe speed, and exercise due care.

(g) It is pertinent to note that the role of the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) is not limited to providing compensation to victims.
It also serves a preventive function, sending a clear message to all road users that negligent and rash driving will be held accountable.

While the accident has already been established as having occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle, it cannot be ignored that the claimant, despite the ease of access to the foot over bridge, opted to cross the road amidst high-speed traffic, thereby knowingly exposing himself to danger.

It is the responsibility of the Tribunal not only to ensure that drivers adhere to traffic rules and avoid speeding, but also to emphasize that pedestrians must exercise due care while crossing roads.
Safe pedestrian behavior is a matter of self-discipline and public awareness; the Tribunal cannot reiterate it in every instance, but it remains a fundamental aspect of road safety.

Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

"(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166, the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be,
each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be: Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X.
(2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award.

(3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct."

sentences.text: Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance.
The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just.
What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question.
There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb.
Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations.
It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any.
Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration.

Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal,
the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims, wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..."

"9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;

In the present case, considering the driver's lack of prior experience, admitted during cross-examination, coupled with the high-performance nature of the KTM motorcycle, it is evident that the driver's control over the vehicle was insufficient for the traffic conditions on the inner Ring Road, a major arterial road connecting different parts of Delhi and carrying significant traffic volumes at all hours.

(g) It is pertinent to note that the role of the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) is not limited to providing compensation to victims.

It is the responsibility of the Tribunal not only to ensure that drivers adhere to traffic rules and avoid speeding, but also to emphasize that pedestrians must exercise due care while crossing roads.

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b),
(iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of lump sum amounts with reference to circumstances such as age, nature of injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant."
It is settled proposition of law as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident.
Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive, and the victims who have to face their lives.
16. Loss of Earning (a) There is nothing on record to establish the income or employment of the injured person.
(c) Although no detailed medical documents have been filed to indicate the full duration of recovery,
it is reasonable to infer that the injured would have been substantially incapacitated for a period following the accident, considering the severity of the fractures and the need for proper healing.
It is also well-settled that attendant charges are payable even in the absence of documentary proof, and such compensation is admissible even when the services are rendered by family members.
It is well settled that compensation for pain and suffering cannot be measured in exact monetary terms and has to be assessed on the basis of the overall impact on the injured.
It is settled that any fixed rate of interest cannot be prescribed for all cases at all times and would largely depend upon the prevailing rate of interest as per the applicable guidelines.
The exceptions cannot be taken aid of in the course of an argument to seek absolution from liability.
Use of a vehicle in a public place without a permit is a fundamental statutory infraction.
The said situations cannot be equated with absence of licence or a fake licence or a licence for different kind of vehicle, or, for that MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Page No. 24 of 27 (rpt) matter, violation of a condition of carrying more number of passengers.
That apart,
the insurer had taken the plea that the vehicle in question had no permit.
It does not require the wisdom of the "Tripitaka", that the existence of a permit of any nature is a matter of documentary evidence.
Nothing has been brought on record by the insured to prove that he had a permit of the vehicle.
In such a situation, the onus cannot be cast on the insurer.
